I've written notes on all 31 verses. Before you use them, you should know two things.

- **Missing perspectives.** My search tool hit its usage limit before I could reach the modern-scholarship sites (netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org) or the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org). The only Catholic/Orthodox-type material below is what John Gill reports about the early church fathers. None of the sources I read discussed prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
- **Cut-off pages.** The Ellicott and Gill chapter pages stopped loading partway through: Ellicott at v. 21 and Gill at v. 20. Notes for later verses come from other pages.

One more caution: on Bible Hub's Ellicott page, the notes on vv. 18–21 (such as Jethro as "a second Melchizedek") read more like the Pulpit Commentary. I've credited them to the page they appear on.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Ellicott thinks Moses meant it as a firm belief that he wouldn't be heard, and calls his faith weak. The people might fairly have doubted, since no one had seen an appearance of God in over 400 years. Ellicott adds that miracles tend to cluster around turning points in God's dealings with people. (ELL) Guzik says Moses's first question in 3:11 was reasonable. Once God had promised "I will be with you," though, this "But" showed unbelief more than honest seeking. (EW)

**v. 2:** Guzik draws the lesson that God uses what is already in our hand. Moses's 40 years as a shepherd weren't wasted, and God used his shepherd's staff rather than a royal sceptre. He compares Shamgar, David, Samson and the boy with the loaves. (EW) Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary both think it was most likely a plain walking staff of the kind an old man would need. They doubt it was an Egyptian official's rod kept from his time at court. (ELL; PUL)

**v. 3:** The Hebrew word for "snake" is a general one and doesn't name a species. Ellicott takes Moses's honest record of running away as a sign of an eyewitness author. (ELL) Guzik stresses that it became a real, frightening snake. (EW)

**v. 4:** People who handle snakes grab them by the neck, so being told to take it by the tail tested Moses's faith and courage. Ellicott's phrase is that "faith triumphed over instinct." (ELL) Guzik says Moses learned to obey even when it was uncomfortable. (EW)

**v. 5:** Ellicott says this verse shows that miracles are given mainly to prove that someone is God's messenger. (ELL) Pulpit says the sign was meant to convince Israel. Before Pharaoh it would test him, not convince him. (PUL) Guzik says it would show the people that the covenant God had not abandoned them. (EW)

**v. 6:** This was white leprosy, which was thought incurable. Both Ellicott and Gill suggest it may be the origin of later pagan stories (Manetho, Tacitus and others) that the Israelites were driven out of Egypt as "lepers." (ELL; GILL) Pulpit says making the disease appear and vanish instantly went against all experience. (PUL)

**v. 7:** Guzik notes that the first two signs both turned something good into something evil and then back again. He reads the message to Moses himself as "your enemies can be made powerless" and "your pollution can be made pure." (EW)

**v. 8:** On "the voice of the first sign," Ellicott says the sign itself speaks. If people who knew snake-charmers' tricks weren't moved by the first sign, the second would persuade most of them. His comment: "God is patient with all reasonable doubt." (ELL)

**v. 9:** In Ellicott's reading, the rod-to-snake sign shows a weak tool becoming a power to punish, and the hand shows a mission both to punish and to save. The blood points to Egypt's peace turning into disaster. (ELL) Guzik says the third sign is pure judgment, and unlike the first two it isn't reversed. (EW)

**v. 10:** The Hebrew means "no man of words" and "heavy of mouth/tongue." Ellicott mentions a Jewish tradition that Moses couldn't pronounce labial sounds such as b, m and p. (ELL; EW) Gill thinks he had a real speech impediment. Calvin says Moses was never eloquent and wasn't given new eloquence. Constable and Bridgeway see the claim as an excuse, noting that Acts 7:22 calls Moses eloquent. (SL10) GotQuestions says a stutter or other disfluency is possible but can't be known. (https://www.gotquestions.org/did-Moses-stutter.html)

**v. 11:** Gill says that since God made the mouth and gave the senses, he can remove any impediment. Their defects also fall under his good pleasure. (GILL) Guzik says the point isn't to explain where evil comes from, and there's no fatalism in it. God is mighty enough to work through anyone who makes himself available. (EW)

**v. 12:** God will supply the words and help Moses speak. Ellicott compares Matthew 10:19–20 and Jeremiah 1:6–9. (ELL)

**v. 13:** Ellicott reads it as "pray send by whom thou wilt," calling it "curt, impatient, and scarcely reverent." (ELL) Guzik says this showed Moses's real problem: he was unwilling, not unable. (EW) Gill reports that many early church fathers read "him whom thou wilt send" as the Messiah. His own suggestion is that it may be a reluctant "let Him send whom He will." (GILL)

**v. 14:** Guzik notes that God was angry only now, at plain unwillingness. He sees Aaron as more a discipline than a help, pointing to the golden calf and to Numbers 12. (EW) Pulpit thinks the anger means displeasure, and the "punishment" was that the role was split between two men. It also suggests that "the Levite" looks ahead to the priestly tribe. (PUL) Wesley says that even self-distrust displeases God when it gets in the way of duty. (WES) Ellicott thinks "can speak well" means easy speech rather than excellent speech. (ELL)

**v. 15:** Moses would supply the content and Aaron the wording. God would be with both mouths. (ELL)

**v. 16:** Ellicott says God spoke to Aaron only through Moses, so Moses kept the higher place. (ELL) Pulpit says divine inspiration would rest on Moses, and Aaron should take his words as God's. (PUL) Gill reports Jewish readings that "as God" means "master," or "prince" (Onkelos's paraphrase), and links it to judges being called "gods" in Psalm 82. (GILL)

**v. 17:** Both commentaries say "this staff" means the very rod that had become a snake, and "signs" means the signs still to come. (ELL; PUL)

**v. 18:** Guzik says the call of God doesn't remove ordinary courtesy toward a father-in-law, and Moses kept the full story to himself. (EW) Bible Hub's Ellicott page says Moses rightly gave only one of his motives. It praises Jethro as kind and gracious and calls him a kind of "second Melchizedek." (ELL)

**v. 19:** The page says Moses seems to have delayed, so God's "Go, return" is a firm order. Those who wanted him dead included the victim's relatives and officials, not just Pharaoh. (ELL)

**v. 20:** Pulpit thinks the sons were Gershom and the infant Eliezer, and that Zipporah and the baby probably rode while Gershom walked. (PUL) "The rod of God" is the staff that God's power had made his instrument. (ELL; WES)

**v. 21:** Ellicott identifies three phases. First Pharaoh's heart was simply unmoved. Then he hardened it himself. Only after that did God harden it as a judgment. (ELL) Pulpit sees it as the natural punishment of sin under God's moral government, not a miraculous intervention. (PUL) Guzik, quoting Augustine, says God never hardened Pharaoh against his will. He gave Pharaoh over to what he already wanted. (EW)

**v. 22:** Pulpit notes that Egyptian kings called themselves "son of the Sun," so the language would sound familiar to Pharaoh. "Firstborn" marks Israel as the one nation God adopted and took into covenant. This is the first mention of Israel's sonship. (PUL) Guzik sees a coming exchange: God's firstborn for Egypt's firstborn. (EW)

**v. 23:** Pulpit says the threat is fulfilled in 12:29. Moses held it back until his last meeting with Pharaoh. (PUL)

**v. 24:** Most writers think God struck Moses with a sudden, life-threatening illness for not circumcising his son (Ellicott, Barnes, Geneva, Matthew Henry). Benson and Poole mention a threatening figure with a drawn sword. The Greek Old Testament (LXX) and the Targum say "angel of the LORD." (BH24) Keil and Delitzsch say Moses first had to prove himself faithful in his own house. (BH24) Calvin reads "met" as a hostile encounter. (SL24) Guzik describes a leader being confronted over a compromise and not allowed to go further until it's dealt with. (EW)

**v. 25:** Writers split on Zipporah's tone. Some hear disgust: Barnes, Ellicott ("causes the blood of his children to be shed"), Pulpit and Coffman. Others hear something positive. Gill says she was thankful she had "bought" her husband back. Keil and Kurtz say she won him back from death by her son's blood. (BH25; SL25) Keil insists "his feet" means Moses's feet, not the child's. Pulpit notes stone knives were considered purer. (BH25) GotQuestions calls her words a lament, something like "a husband of horrors." (https://www.gotquestions.org/bridegroom-of-blood.html)

**v. 26:** Pulpit and Matthew Henry say that once the rite was done, God's anger stopped and Moses recovered. Henry thinks Moses probably sent his family back to Jethro at this point. (PUL; SL25) Constable thinks Zipporah gave up her claim on Moses so he was free for God's service. (SL25)

**v. 27:** Guzik says Aaron's arrival shows God keeping his promise from v. 14. (EW) Matthew Henry says the more clearly the brothers saw God bringing them together, the happier the meeting was. (BH24)

**vv. 28–30:** Guzik quotes F.B. Meyer: Aaron spoke well but was a weak man. (EW)

**v. 31:** Guzik says this fulfils 3:18. Israel had once rejected Moses, but now the time was right. (EW) Matthew Henry says things often go more easily than expected when we take on God's work, and asks how much more we should welcome the good news of redemption. (BH24)

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 21 (hardening Pharaoh's heart)** is the clearest disagreement I found.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan:** Wesley says that only after Pharaoh had hardened his own heart many times would God "permit Satan" to harden it fully. On 8:15 and 8:32 he says Pharaoh did it himself, and God only by not stopping him. (WES) J.D. Walt of Seedbed, writing on 7:3, says God allows people to go their own way rather than actively hardening them. Saying God willed the hardness would mean God also willed the suffering that followed. (https://seedbed.com/i-will-harden-pharaohs-heart-on-sovereignty-freedom-and-the-will-of-god/)
- **Reformed/Baptist:** John Piper argues that God's hardening in Romans 9:18 is unconditional. He rejects the view that God hardens only those who first hardened themselves, a view he quotes from Stott and Morris. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-hardening-of-pharaoh-and-the-hope-of-the-world) A Gospel Coalition article quotes Piper that in Exodus 4–14 the hardening is never grounded in anything Pharaoh did, but in God's purpose. It also says God never hardens true believers. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/you-asked-does-god-harden-a-believers-heart/) D.A. Carson takes a middle position. Pharaoh was already wicked, so this was a judgment, and "God hardened" and "Pharaoh hardened" fit together. (https://www.monergism.com/blog/%E2%80%9Ci-will-harden-his-heart-so-he-will-not-let-people-go%E2%80%9D) Paul Carter (TGC Canada) notes that God isn't said to act on Pharaoh's heart until chapter 9. He calls the hardening temporary and for a specific purpose, not eternal rejection. (https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/did-god-harden-pharaohs-heart/)
- **Pentecostal list (Enduring Word):** Guzik, following Augustine, says God hardens only by withholding mercy, never against Pharaoh's will. (EW)

**vv. 24–26 (the bridegroom of blood):**
- **Lutheran:** A 1517 article reads Zipporah's act as law and gospel. Zipporah held the blood up to remind God of his promise, just as Jesus stands between us and God's anger. Christ is the true "Bridegroom of Blood," and baptism replaces circumcision. It also takes "feet" as a polite word for genitals. (https://www.1517.org/articles/bridegroom-of-blood)
- **Reformed (TGC):** Paul Carter says the Hebrew word can mean "kinsman" as well as "bridegroom." He thinks Zipporah more likely touched Gershom in a Midianite rite of joining the family, and that God accepted it as done in faith. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/moses-zipporah-strangest-circumcision-story-exodus/)
- **Evangelical (bible.org):** Zipporah is presented as someone who did exactly what God required at the right moment. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/23884)

---

## 3. Other views
- **The early church fathers on v. 13:** Gill reports that many of them read "send whom you will send" as Moses asking God to send the Messiah. (GILL)
- **Older critical scholarship on v. 24:** The Cambridge Bible calls the passage an ancient story with "strongly anthropomorphic" language, meaning it describes God in human terms. It quotes McNeile that "sought to kill him" is an old way of saying Moses fell dangerously ill. (BH24) It suggests "blood-bridegroom" may originally have described a bridegroom who was himself circumcised. (BH25) Constable mentions the possibility of an ancient marriage formula tied to circumcision before marriage. (SL25)
